extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, legal professionals, and members of the public researching covered business method (CBM) patents
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions and procedural/ substantive standards governing Covered Business Method (CBM) patents under the America Invents Act, including what counts as a CBM, the 'technological invention' exclusion, PTAB institution standards, and who may petition for CBM review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covered business method (CBM) patent definition (AIA §18)
rubrics_metrics.description: A covered business method (CBM) patent is defined in section 18 of the America Invents Act (AIA) as a patent that "claims a method or corresponding apparatus for performing data processing or other operations used in the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service," but is not for a "technological" invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AIA statute provides for CBM review of CBM patents — an administrative proceeding to determine the validity of the patent under review. Congress created CBM review because of concern with "litigation abuse over business method patents." (Section 18 is implemented by USPTO regulations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: CBM patents must relate to monetary matters (regulatory further definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under USPTO regulations promulgated pursuant to the statute, a CBM patent is one relating to monetary matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO regulations further refine the statutory definition; whether a claim 'relates to monetary matters' is a regulatory criterion used to determine CBM status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological invention exclusion (regulatory test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A technological invention is defined as one in which "the claimed subject matter as a whole recites a technological feature that is novel and unobvious over the prior art; and solves a technical problem using a technical solution."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed subject matter satisfies this test it is considered a technological invention and thus excluded from being a CBM. The technological-invention inquiry is central to distinguishing CBM patents from technological patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial Practice Guide anti-technological example: mere recitation of known technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere recitation of known technologies, such as computer hardware, communication or computer networks, software, memory, computer-readable storage medium, scanners, display devices or databases, or specialized machines, such as an ATM or point of sale device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO Trial Practice Guide lists these as examples of what is not a technological invention — merely listing known technological components does not make the claimed subject matter a technological invention for purposes of excluding it from CBM review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial Practice Guide anti-technological example: use of known prior art technology to accomplish a process
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting the use of known prior art technology to accomplish a process or method, even if that process or method is novel and non-obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: According to the Trial Practice Guide, employing known technology to carry out a (potentially novel) process does not convert the claim into a technological invention; this is an anti-feature of being 'technological.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial Practice Guide anti-technological example: predictable combination of prior art structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining prior art structures to achieve the normal, expected, or predictable result of that combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Guide treats predictable combinations of prior art structures that yield expected results as non-technological; such combinations do not meet the regulatory technological-invention test.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB institution standard for CBM proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard for whether the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) will institute a CBM proceeding is whether a petition by an interested party establishes that it is more likely than not that at least one claim of the challenged patent is unpatentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'more likely than not' threshold governs institution of CBM review (see 35 U.S.C. § 324). Petitions are ordinarily filed by parties sued for infringement, but standing rules (see separate criterion) can broaden who may file.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of invalidity grounds in CBM review
rubrics_metrics.description: Any statutory ground of invalidity may be considered in CBM review, including patent ineligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although consideration of certain grounds (e.g., § 101) was once contested, it is now established that CBM proceedings may address any statutory invalidity ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing / who may petition for CBM review
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition is typically filed by an interested party (ordinarily, a party that the patentee sued for patent infringement); the PTAB has held that a supplier whose customer has been sued for patent infringement also has standing to petition for a CBM review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB decisions (e.g., SAP America v. Pi-Net; Liberty Mutual v. Progressive) and congressional discussion indicate that parties beyond the direct defendant — such as suppliers with customers sued for infringement — can qualify as interested parties for CBM petitions.
